To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effective doses from dental CT scans on 10 and 14 year old children were similar to those for adults.
the effective doses to 10 year old phantoms are 1.5 times those to adolescent phantoms for the same imaging protocol.
the effective doses to 10 year old children and adolescent patients are similar to adult values.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method for estimating organ and effective doses to paediatric patients undergoing dental CBCT.
the use of dental cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) for the diagnosis of oral diseases.
the development of new technologies and techniques for improving the quality of medical images and reducing the radiation dose to patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the radiation risks from dental CBCT are higher than for adult patients, but are still small compared with the risk from natural radiation.
the effective dose to a 10 year child is similar to that to an adult, whereas the effective dose to an adolescent is about 70% of that of an adult.
the effective dose to a 10 year child is similar to that to an adult but the percentage lifetime mortality risks to a child is considerably greater.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of paediatric phantoms is essential in estimating the organ and effective doses and the radiation risks for paediatric dental CBCT.
paediatric effective doses from dental CT are similar to adult values, and therefore it is imperative that dose optimisation and justification are performed for each patient.
paediatric effective doses are higher than adult doses, but the lifetime attributable mortality risks are similar.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the radiation risks to children from dental CBCT is significantly higher than for adult patients and that the radiation risks from dental CBCT to children is not insignificant.
paediatric doses from dental CB CT should be estimated using age specific phantoms and that the effective dose and lifetime mortality risks are considerably higher for young children than for adults.
the effective dose to the 10 years old phantom was 1.5 times higher than the dose to the adolescent phantom, which is contrary to the findings from adult studies.
